body_markdown:
Employee reimbursement is how a company pays staff back for business expenses they covered with their own money. A cash advance works the other way around: the company releases the funds first, and the employee accounts for them afterwards in a liquidation report.


Both are simple to run when a team is small. As a company grows, employees wait longer to be repaid and finance sees the spending only after the paperwork arrives.


This guide covers how reimbursements and cash advances work in the Philippines, what a liquidation report should contain, what the BIR requires, and how to reduce the number of claims your team has to file.


## **Reimbursement vs cash advance**


Most companies use both. The choice usually comes down to the size of the expense and whether it can be planned ahead, since it is hard to ask an employee to front the cost of say, a provincial trip.


Here is how the two compare on the points that usually cause trouble.


Factor


Reimbursement


Cash advance


Who puts up the money


The employee


The company


When the paperwork is due


Before the employee is paid back


After the spend, by a deadline you set


Main document


Reimbursement form with invoices attached


Liquidation report with invoices attached


What usually goes wrong


Employees wait weeks for their own money


Advances stay open for months


Best suited to


Small, occasional spending


Planned trips, events and field work


If documents are missing


The company can decline the claim


Any balance not returned can be treated as the employee's taxable income


Neither one is the same as petty cash, which is a fixed fund kept in the office for small purchases. We covered that separately in our[guide to petty cash](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/petty-cash?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) .


## **What goes in a liquidation report**


A liquidation report is the employee's accounting of a cash advance. It shows how much was released, what it was spent on, and how much is left to return (or how much the company still owes, if the employee went over). Private companies generally design their own format, but a usable one has these parts:


- Employee name, department and the date filed
- The cash advance reference and the amount released
- The purpose, such as a client visit or a provincial trip
- Each expense on its own line, with the date, supplier, invoice number and amount
- Total spent, and the balance to return or to be reimbursed
- Signatures of the employee and the approver


A simple liquidation report for a ₱10,000 advance would look something like this.


Date


Particulars


Invoice no.

₱2,400

Attach the invoices behind the report in the same order as the lines. It sounds minor, but it saves whoever reviews it a good amount of time.


Some expenses come with no invoice at all, like tricycle fares or a parking attendant with no booklet. For those, many companies use a reimbursement expense receipt (RER), a short form the employee signs to certify the amount and what it was for. Keep it for small amounts only. An RER is an internal document, so it will not carry the same weight as a supplier's invoice if the expense is ever questioned.


### **What the BIR looks at**


Two things:


The first is whose name is on the invoice. Since the Ease of Paying Taxes Act, the[invoice is the primary proof of a purchase](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/sales-invoice-vs-official-receipt?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) for goods and services alike. For the company to deduct the expense and claim the input VAT, the invoice should be issued to the company. An invoice made out to the employee personally can get the expense[disallowed for both income tax and VAT](https://www.pwc.com/ph/en/tax/tax-publications/taxwise-or-otherwise/2025/beyond-paychecks-the-dilemma-of-employee-reimbursements.html?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) . PwC suggests giving employees a small reference card with the company's registered name, address and TIN to hand to the cashier.


The second is whether the payment counts as the employee's income. Under Revenue Regulations No. 2-98, advances and reimbursements are[not treated as compensation](https://www.grantthornton.com.ph/insights/articles-and-updates1/lets-talk-tax/bir-assessments-related-to-employee-reimbursements/?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) when the expense is an ordinary and necessary cost of the business and the employee is required to liquidate it. If an advance is not liquidated and the excess is not returned, that excess becomes taxable income of the employee.


Withholding on reimbursed expenses is its own topic and depends on your taxpayer classification, so check that part with your accountant.


## **Where the process usually breaks**


Late liquidation is the most common problem. An account manager takes an advance for a Cebu trip in March, gets pulled into the next project, and the advance is still open in June. On the books that is a receivable from an employee, and it tends to grow without anyone noticing.


Personal cards carrying company spending is the other big one, and marketing teams know it well. Facebook and Google ads get charged to a manager's own credit card because the company has no card of its own, and the amounts are not small. The invoices come out in the wrong name. The company also has no view of the spending until the claim arrives, which could be a month later. Software subscriptions often end up the same way.


And then there are the receipts themselves. Thermal paper fades, and Grab receipts sit in someone's personal email.


A few rules take care of most of this, and they do not need a long policy document:


- A spending limit per claim. Anything above it needs approval before the spend, not after
- A filing deadline. Five working days after the trip or purchase is a reasonable place to start
- A fixed payout schedule, for example every 15th and 30th with payroll, so employees know when their money is coming
- No new cash advance while an old one is still unliquidated
- No invoice in the company's name, no reimbursement, with the RER as the only exception


The fourth rule is the one people push back on the most. It is also the one that clears old advances fastest. On the last rule, Grant Thornton's tax team recommends the same thing: do not reimburse expenses that fail the invoicing requirements.


## **Fewer reimbursements, faster payouts**


Rules keep the queue manageable. To make it shorter, the company has to pay for more things directly, so there is nothing to reimburse afterwards. Company cards do that, although a[corporate credit card from a bank](https://www.paymongo.com/blog/corporate-credit-card-philippines-requirements-how-to-apply?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) needs a credit line and a fair amount of paperwork.


[PayMongo Virtual Cards](https://www.paymongo.com/products/issuing/virtual-cards?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) are a prepaid alternative. They are Mastercard cards funded from your PayMongo Wallet, so there is no credit line to apply for. You can create a card for one person, for a team, or for a single purpose like ad spend. Each card gets its own limit, and you can pause or cancel it from the dashboard. Transactions appear in the dashboard as they happen, under the card that made them.


In practice this takes the largest items out of the reimbursement queue: ads, software, cloud hosting, and flights or hotels booked online. The cards are virtual for now, which means they are for online payments. A client lunch paid at the counter will still go through a claim. For the claims that remain, the slow part is often the payout, with accounting sending bank transfers one at a time.[PayMongo Disbursements](https://www.paymongo.com/products/money-movement/disbursements?ref=paymongo-blog.ghost.io) lets you upload one file with up to 2,500 payouts and send them through InstaPay or PESONet. The 15th and 30th run becomes one task.


## **Keep company spending on company money**


Reimbursements will not disappear completely, and they do not need to. Start with the expenses that are already online, give each one its own card, and keep the liquidation report for what is left.

## **Frequently asked questions**


#### ****Is employee reimbursement taxable in the Philippines?****


Generally no, as long as the expense was an ordinary and necessary business cost and the employee liquidated it with proper documents. An advance that is not liquidated and not returned can be treated as the employee's taxable income.


#### ****What is the difference between reimbursement and liquidation?****


Reimbursement is the company paying an employee back for something they paid for themselves. Liquidation is the employee accounting for money the company gave them in advance.


#### ****What if an employee loses the receipt?****


Ask the supplier for a copy of the invoice first, since some suppliers can reissue or certify one. If that is not possible, your policy can allow an RER or a signed explanation for small amounts. Keep in mind the company may not be able to deduct an expense that has no valid invoice behind it.
